title: Five loaves; bread of life; sealed by the Father (John 6:6–37)
english: So that they may not suppose Andrew hides something for his own need, he said that a child still has five barley loaves and two fish. He said this lest he seem to be hiding what he had for some private need.

He counts only the men, according to the law's custom: those who have nothing childish or womanish, but a youthful mind, whom he also feeds with the bread that strengthens the heart and fills with delight.

For this reason he gives thanks: lest he seem opposed to God, and that he may teach us to give thanks when we eat; yet also as man he gives thanks, that until the passion he may escape the notice of the ruler of this age.

Christ feeds the faithful through the five barley loaves, which signify the coarser teaching of the Pentateuch, and through the two fish, which are the apostolic teaching of the evangelical and apostolic proclamation.
Through the sign he teaches them to take heart in him and not to lose heart in distress, or not to shrink from hospitality, but to be bold toward the good.
He does not forbid working, but worrying and fretting about tomorrow, that he may dry up in advance the heresy of the Messalians and Manichaeans who use no handiwork at all.
He means the intelligible, rational, and spiritual food that remains; for this helps us enjoy the goods to come, which faith in Christ procures.
He means the mystical participation which the Son has given, that sanctifies soul and body, weaving the human together with what befits God.

He "sealed" him—that is, anointed with the Holy Spirit the Lord's human flesh, not the Godhead; for almost all the names of the economy are taken concerning the flesh. He said this either because he is naturally formed toward the Father, that is, anointed (for those anointed are sealed), or "sealed" means the Father confirmed or undeniably disclosed the Son by his own witness; for the Son is impress and seal of the Father's essence, seen without difference as the Father.
Even if he knew those people would gain nothing, still for the common benefit of the teaching he answered.
It is not the one serving the shadows of the law who does God's will, but the one who believes in Christ.

He did not say this as if the manna food were a lie, but because that was a type, not itself the truth. Christ is the manna who is life by nature and gives life to all things—that is, bread as feeding soul and body.

Here again he calls the bread—that is, the flesh—from heaven, not because it was from heaven, but because it was united to the Word who came down from heaven; and after the union the saints speak without distinction as of one person and one hypostasis, even though they know the difference even after the union of flesh, soul, and Godhead.

For he frees from sins and makes friends of God and partakers of the "divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4) and frees from Gehenna and counts the worthy worthy of the kingdom—those who share as they ought in the flesh of the Word of God; for all these are life and food of the immortal soul.
He is bread of life not as soothing bodily hunger, but remaking the whole living being from end to end into life, through the spiritual words of which we are filled, which is life.
Water and drink here mean either sanctification through the Spirit or the Holy Spirit himself.
"All that the Father gives me will come to me" (John 6:37). Faith in him is no chance matter, but needs a tilt from above and a soul noble, God-minded, and grateful that receives faith, the Father's
